key_terms.meaning: I(x) = log₂(1/P(x)) bits; a less likely symbol carries more information
Average self-information per symbol, H(X) = Σ P(xᵢ) log₂(1/P(xᵢ)) bits/symbol
R = r_s × H bits per second, where r_s is the symbols per second
Mapping source symbols to binary codewords so the average length L̄ is close to H
No codeword is the beginning of another, so the stream decodes without commas
A prefix code with lengths lᵢ exists only if Σ 2^(−lᵢ) ≤ 1
η = H / L̄, and redundancy = 1 − η, with L̄ the average codeword length
I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X), the uncertainty the output removes
Channel set by transition probabilities P(yⱼ|xᵢ); each use is independent of earlier ones
Two inputs, two outputs, correct with probability 1 − p and flipped with probability p
C = max over input distributions of I(X;Y), the highest reliable rate in bits per channel use
C = B log₂(1 + S/N), with B in hertz and S/N a plain power ratio
Any rate R < C can be sent with as small an error probability as we like; above C it cannot
R = k/n for an (n, k) code: k message bits carried by n transmitted bits
Codeword c = mG and every codeword satisfies cHᵀ = 0
S = rHᵀ = eHᵀ; it depends only on the error pattern e, not on the message sent
A linear block code where every cyclic shift of a codeword is also a codeword, built from g(x)
In a convolutional code, the number of shift-register stages that one input bit influences
Decoder uses the analogue received values (or their reliabilities) instead of hard 0/1 decisions

takeaways: Information depends only on probability: a sure symbol (P = 1) tells you nothing, so its self-information is zero.
Entropy is largest when all symbols are equally likely and equals log₂ M for M equally likely symbols.
Huffman coding always gives the smallest average length among prefix codes for a given set of probabilities.
Mutual information measures what the channel output tells you about the input; it is zero when input and output are independent.
For a band-limited AWGN channel the capacity grows only logarithmically with power but linearly with bandwidth.
The channel coding theorem promises small error probability below capacity but gives no construction; the codes in 7.6 to 7.9 are that construction.
Syndrome decoding turns error correction into a table lookup on the error pattern, which is far smaller than the set of received words.
Cyclic codes allow encoder and syndrome circuit to be built from shift registers and XOR gates, which is why they appear in hardware.
Long blocks with soft iterative decoding (turbo, LDPC) get within a fraction of a decibel of the Shannon limit.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always pair a derivation (entropy, mutual information, capacity) with a numerical exercise (Huffman tree, syndrome, trellis), so prepare both the proof and the arithmetic.

bank.q: Define self-information and entropy for a discrete memoryless source. Derive the expression for entropy and show that it is maximum when all symbols are equally likely.
outline: Self-information I(xᵢ) = log₂(1/P(xᵢ)) with the three properties: zero for certain events, decreases as probability rises, additive for independent events
Entropy H = Σ P(xᵢ) log₂(1/P(xᵢ)) bits/symbol
Maximum by Jensen's inequality or by the log inequality; H ≤ log₂ M with equality at P = 1/M
One numerical check with a two-symbol source

bank.q: State the source coding theorem. Explain Shannon–Fano coding and Huffman coding, and list the differences between them.
outline: Source coding theorem: L̄ can be made as close to H as we wish but never below it, with H ≤ L̄ < H + 1
Shannon–Fano: sort probabilities, split into two groups of nearly equal total probability, assign 0 and 1, recurse
Huffman: repeatedly merge the two smallest probabilities, build the tree upward, read codes from root to leaf
Shannon–Fano is not always optimal; Huffman is optimal for a given symbol set, but needs the whole tree at the encoder

bank.q: Define mutual information for a discrete memoryless channel and prove I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X). Also define the binary symmetric channel.
outline: Joint entropy H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) = H(Y) + H(X|Y)
I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X,Y)
BSC transition matrix with crossover probability p; symmetry gives H(Y|X) = H(p)
I(X;Y) = 0 when input and output are independent; maximum for equiprobable input

bank.q: State the channel coding theorem and explain its meaning and its limitations.
outline: Statement: for R < C, codes exist with arbitrarily small error probability; for R > C the error probability cannot be made to vanish
Applies to long blocks, so the decoder may be complex and the delay large
Does not tell us how to build the code; that is the job of the later sections
Contrast with the source coding theorem

bank.q: A source has six symbols with probabilities 0.4, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.1, 0.05. Construct a Huffman code, find the average codeword length, the entropy, the efficiency and the redundancy.
outline: Correct merging order and the resulting tree
Codeword lengths and the average L̄ = Σ pᵢ lᵢ
Entropy H computed symbol by symbol in bits
Efficiency η = H/L̄ as a percentage and redundancy 1 − η
Check Kraft inequality Σ 2^(−lᵢ) ≤ 1

bank.q: A binary symmetric channel has crossover probability p = 0.01. Find the channel capacity in bits per channel use for equiprobable input, and the capacity when p = 0.5. Comment.
outline: C = 1 − H(p) for the BSC, with H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1 − p) log₂(1 − p)
Evaluate H(0.01) ≈ 0.08 bits, so C ≈ 0.92 bits per use
At p = 0.5 the output is independent of the input and C = 0
Comment: the channel is useless at p = 0.5, and a p near 1 is as good as p near 0 because the errors can be inverted

bank.q: For the (7,4) Hamming code, write the generator and parity-check matrices, encode the message 1011, and use the syndrome to correct the received word 1011011.
outline: G in systematic form [I₄ | P] and H = [Pᵀ | I₃]
c = mG, giving the seven-bit codeword
Syndrome S = rHᵀ and the single-error syndrome table
Identify the error position and flip that bit
State d_min = 3, so the code corrects one error per word

bank.q: A cyclic code uses generator polynomial g(x) = 1 + x + x³ over GF(2). Encode the message polynomial 1 + x² by polynomial division and find the syndrome when the received word is 1100101.
outline: Multiply m(x) by x^(n−k) and divide by g(x) to get the remainder as parity bits
Codeword is the remainder appended to the message
Received polynomial divided by g(x) gives the syndrome polynomial
Non-zero syndrome points to the error; the syndrome circuit is a shift register with feedback taps at g(x)

bank.q: A rate-1/2 convolutional code with constraint length 3 has generators 101 and 111. Draw the encoder, the state diagram and the trellis, and decode the received sequence 11 01 11 10 by the Viterbi algorithm.
outline: Shift register with two memory stages and two modulo-2 adders
State transition table and the trellis for at least four time steps
Add-compare-select metric update at each step
Survivor path and traceback to the most likely input bits
Free distance and the number of errors it can correct

bank.q: A channel has bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio S/N. Using C = B log₂(1 + S/N), examine how doubling the bandwidth compares with doubling the transmitted power. Support your answer with numbers.
outline: Doubling B roughly doubles C when S/N is fixed
Doubling S/N adds B log₂(1 + 2S/N) − B log₂(1 + S/N), which is less than a doubling
As B → ∞ with fixed total power, C tends to 1.44 S/N₀
Practical conclusion: bandwidth is the cheaper resource for capacity, power the dearer one

bank.q: Compare Hamming, BCH, turbo and LDPC codes on rate, block length, decoding complexity and error performance, and state where each is used.
outline: Hamming: small block, single-error correction, trivial hardware, used in memory and simple links
BCH: multiple-error correction, algebraic decoding, used in storage and older satellite links
Turbo: parallel concatenated codes with iterative soft decoding, close to the Shannon limit, used in 3G/4G
LDPC: sparse parity-check matrix, belief propagation, used in 5G, Wi-Fi and deep-space
Trade-off: long blocks and soft information buy performance at the cost of delay and complexity

bank.q: Show that the average length of any prefix code cannot be less than the source entropy. Discuss what the extra length costs in a practical system.
outline: Use Kraft inequality and the log-sum inequality to show L̄ ≥ H
Equality holds when all lᵢ = −log₂ pᵢ, that is, probabilities are powers of two
The gap H ≤ L̄ < H + 1 comes from rounding lengths to whole bits
Extra bits mean extra bandwidth or storage, visible on a UPI transaction record or a call bill

bank.q: A system must deliver a bit error rate of 10⁻⁵ over a channel of known capacity. Using the channel coding theorem and the behaviour of convolutional and LDPC codes, judge whether the requirement can be met, and what happens if the code rate is chosen above capacity.
outline: Compare the proposed code rate R with C; R < C is the necessary condition
Channel coding theorem: existence, not construction; long blocks and soft decoding bring practice near the bound
Above capacity no code works: the error probability tends to a floor no matter the decoder
Convolutional with Viterbi gives about 2 dB coding gain at hard decision, more with soft decision; LDPC gains more
Practical limits: delay, decoder complexity, and the gap to the Shannon limit in decibels

glossary.def: Unit of information when the logarithm is taken to base 2; one fair coin toss carries one bit.
The information in one outcome of probability P, equal to log₂(1/P) bits.
The average information per source symbol, the minimum average number of bits needed to describe it.
Number of source symbols produced per second, measured in baud or symbols per second.
Entropy multiplied by the symbol rate, in bits per second.
A code in which no codeword is a prefix of another, so decoding needs no separators.
The condition Σ 2^(−lᵢ) ≤ 1 that a set of codeword lengths must satisfy for a prefix code to exist.
Entropy divided by average codeword length, usually quoted as a percentage.
The reduction in uncertainty about the input caused by observing the output, in bits per channel use.
The uncertainty of the input and output taken together, H(X,Y).
The uncertainty left in the input after the output is known, H(X|Y), also called equivocation.
A channel with finite input and output alphabets whose behaviour at each use is fixed and independent of past uses.
A two-input two-output channel that flips the bit with probability p and passes it with probability 1 − p.
The maximum mutual information over all input distributions, in bits per channel use.
The minimum signal-to-noise ratio per bit, about −1.6 dB, below which reliable communication is impossible however long the code.
A code that maps each group of k message bits to one fixed block of n transmitted bits.
Weight is the number of ones in a word; distance is the number of positions in which two words differ.
The smallest Hamming distance between any two codewords; a code with d_min corrects t = ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋ errors.
The k × n matrix G whose rows span the code, so a codeword is c = mG.
The (n − k) × n matrix H orthogonal to every codeword, satisfying cHᵀ = 0.
The (n − k)-bit vector S = rHᵀ, which is zero for a valid codeword and depends only on the error pattern.
The polynomial g(x) of degree n − k that divides xⁿ − 1 and whose multiples are exactly the codewords of a cyclic code.
The number of input bits, including the current one, that influence any single output bit of a convolutional code.
A time-indexed diagram of the encoder states and allowed transitions, used by the Viterbi decoder.
Decoding that uses quantised received amplitudes instead of firm 0/1 decisions, gaining about 2 dB.
